Under the stated assumption, DeepWalk would be treated as a policy over random-walk sequences, and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) would train that policy from pairwise preferences induced by Bradley-Terry human feedback reward modeling. Let a preferred random walk be w^+ and a dispreferred random walk be w^-. A standard DPO objective for DeepWalk would maximize the log-sigmoid of the preference margin between the current walk policy and a fixed reference policy:

L_DPO(θ) = - E[(w^+, w^-)] [ log σ( β [ log π_θ(w^+) - log π_θ(w^-) - log π_ref(w^+) + log π_ref(w^-) ] ) ]

where π_θ is DeepWalk's current random-walk policy, π_ref is a frozen reference policy, σ is the sigmoid function, and β > 0 controls the strength of the preference constraint. Equivalently, minimizing this loss encourages DeepWalk to assign higher probability to human-preferred walks than to rejected walks, relative to the reference model.

If one writes the walk probability as a product of stepwise transition probabilities, then log π_θ(w) is the sum of the log transition probabilities along the walk, so the DPO loss aligns the entire random-walk trajectory rather than individual edges in isolation. In this hypothetical adaptation, the Bradley-Terry model supplies the pairwise preference signal, while DPO converts that signal into a direct policy optimization objective without explicitly fitting a separate reward model at training time.
